summary: Describes using GRE when IP is the delivery protocol, the payload protocol, or both. It also describes using IP addresses and autonomous system numbers as part of a GRE source route. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This note shows how to wrap internet packets inside other internet packets, like a box inside a box.

questions: what ip protocol number does gre use
how does gre source routing work
subtitle: How GRE packets ride inside IP, how IP rides inside GRE, and how IP addresses and AS numbers can form a source route.

tldr.problem: RFC 1701 defined GRE as a way to wrap arbitrary packets in an arbitrary transport protocol, but it did not spell out what that means when the protocol involved is IP itself.
tldr.mechanism: This companion memo says GRE in IP uses IP protocol type 47, IP inside GRE uses Protocol Type 0x800, and it defines source route entries built from IP addresses (Address Family 0x800) or autonomous system numbers (0xfffe).
tldr.outcome: It gives implementers the IPv4-specific rules for GRE. It is an Informational memo, not a standard.

today: RFC 1702 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 1701, the base GRE specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This memo is a companion to RFC 1701, which described GRE, a mechanism for encapsulating arbitrary packets within an arbitrary transport protocol. Here the focus is on IP: IP as the delivery protocol (the outer wrapper), IP as the payload protocol (the thing being carried), and the special case where IP is both.

The memo also describes how IP addresses and autonomous system numbers can be used as part of a GRE source route. It states plainly that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.plainLanguage: GRE is a way to put one kind of packet inside another. This note says how to do it when both the box and the thing in the box are internet packets.

sections.title: IP as Delivery and as Payload
sections.content:
When GRE packets are carried inside IP, they use IP protocol type 47. When IP packets are carried inside GRE, the GRE Protocol Type field is set to 0x800.

When IP is wrapped in IP, the TTL, TOS and IP security options MAY be copied from the payload packet into the same fields of the delivery packet. The payload packet's TTL MUST be decremented when the packet is decapsulated, so that no packet lives forever.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer envelope gets a label saying it holds a GRE packet. The inner packet keeps its own life counter, and that counter must tick down when the envelope is opened so the packet cannot wander forever.

sections.title: Source Route Entries
sections.content:
A source route lets the sender list the stops a packet should visit. In GRE, each list lives in a Source Route Entry (SRE) in the Routing Information field. Each SRE starts with an Address Family, an 8-bit SRE Offset that points to the first octet of the next address or number, and an 8-bit SRE Length giving the total length of the list in octets.

  • Address Family 0x800: the list holds IP addresses and forms an IP source route.
  • Address Family 0xfffe: the list holds autonomous system numbers and forms an AS source route.

A system processing an IP source route MUST use the SRE Offset to find the next destination. If that destination is the system itself, it advances the offset by four, the size of an IP address. For an AS source route the step is two, the size of an AS number. When the offset reaches the SRE Length, the offset in the GRE header should move on to the next SRE, if there is one. This repeats until the next hop is not this system or the whole SRE is used up.

If the route is incomplete, the Strict Source Route bit is checked. For a strict route whose next hop is not adjacent, the IP version says the packet MUST be dropped, and the AS version says it should be dropped. Otherwise the system puts the indicated address into the delivery header's destination and forwards the packet. For AS routes, how an AS number becomes a delivery address is outside the scope of the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: A source route is a list of stops written on the package. Each router crosses off its own name and sends the package to the next one. If the list says to go strictly stop by stop and the next stop is not a neighbor, the package is thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo has nothing to say here. Its Security Considerations section states only that security issues are not discussed. Readers should not take that to mean the mechanisms described are free of security concerns; the RFC simply does not address them.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors did not write anything about safety in this note, so it does not tell us whether these tricks are safe.

references.text: Hanks, S., Li, T, Farinacci, D., and P. Traina, "Generic Routing Encapsulation", RFC 1701, October 1994.
